insights.headline: The exact mechanism of the mission fax board reappears unchanged across three life decades: a handmade tracking board built on the back of a door, then a spreadsheet or wall, each time deployed when the outcome is actually out of his control.
insights.explanation: In E2 he builds a masking-tape grid tracking his district's numbers and his companion's wake-up time, then rebuilds the same board in Ivaiporã. In E3 he keeps a private color-coded spreadsheet of CSM touches nobody asked for, and a sticky-note wall he still keeps 'at my own place.' In E5, facing a medical situation with zero controllable inputs, he builds a Google Sheet with 'a trend line on my son.' The recurrence across a religious mission, a sales job, and a NICU room suggests the board isn't a management tool so much as a fixed response to anxiety, deployed most intensely precisely where he has the least actual leverage.

evidence.quote: I made my own board. On the back of our apartment door with masking tape, a grid, every companionship in my district, every day, every number.

insights.would_predict: Health and Wellness: facing a personal health diagnosis or his own physical symptom (not a family member's), he will start logging metrics (sleep, weight, symptoms) within days rather than waiting on a doctor's plan.

insights.headline: He reads private validation from an authority figure (fax rank, promotion track, president's comments) in the bathroom or in bed, away from witnesses, in at least two experiences.
insights.explanation: In E2 he reads the mission fax in the bathroom 'because it felt weird to be that happy about it in front of everybody,' and in E3 he checks the Salesforce dashboard 'in bed... before Britt woke up.' Both moments are described as almost shameful pleasures, hidden from the people closest to him (fellow missionaries, his wife). This is not simple humility -- it's concealment of a specific kind of appetite (rank, standing) that he elsewhere disclaims wanting.

insights.headline: He repeatedly renounces status just before or after securing it, and reads the resulting relief as confirmation he didn't want it — when the timing suggests engineered plausible deniability.
insights.explanation: In E2 he writes the letter refusing a leadership title two weeks before transfer calls and calls the resulting relief 'the Spirit confirming it.' In E4 he frames leaving the startup as mission-driven ('I couldn't not build it') while the actual trigger was a new VP causing him to feel 'physically sick,' and he retroactively declines the board seat he never got offered a real shot at, saying 'I couldn't get there.' Both times the renunciation happens right at the moment real evaluation (would I actually get the role/deal) is uncertain, letting him keep the identity of someone unattached to status regardless of outcome.

evidence.quote: I sent that letter before transfer calls. Two weeks before.
I probably would've been in the mix. Maybe. There were like two other people who probably would've been in the mix too.

insights.would_predict: Purpose: in a future opportunity for public recognition (award, board seat, keynote), he will preemptively minimize his chances or decline consideration shortly before the actual decision is made, then describe the outcome as relief rather than loss.

insights.headline: When someone under his authority is hurt by his need for control, he reframes their complaint as a misunderstanding of his intentions rather than engaging their account.

facts.what_happened: Speaker was hired as approximately the sixth or seventh sales rep.
Company sold scheduling software for home service businesses (plumbers, HVAC, garage doors).
Speaker hit 143% of quota in first full year, second in the company; Enrique was first with the Texas territory.
Speaker moved from AE to senior AE to team lead to running customer success to director of CS.
Four title changes occurred over five years.
A leaderboard was displayed on a TV by the kitchen.
The leaderboard was later moved into a Salesforce dashboard.
Speaker checked the dashboard at approximately 5:40am.
The overnight data sync ran at 4am, producing fresh numbers each morning.
Speaker eventually had eleven people reporting to them in CS.
Doug, speaker's manager for about a year, wanted to conduct ride-alongs sitting in on speaker's calls; speaker never did one in a year.
Brightway Plumbing was the company's third biggest account, worth $180,000/year, and was assigned to Kaylee, who was about six months into the job.
Brightway had a renewal coming up and their ops manager was expressing dissatisfaction.
Speaker took the account away from Kaylee.
Speaker ran the renewal and the account was saved and upsold to $218,000.
Kaylee quit about four months later.
In her exit interview, Kaylee said something about not being trusted, which speaker heard secondhand.
Speaker rebuilt QBR decks for other CSMs at night and sent them back around 11:40pm with the message "just a couple tweaks!"
Speaker maintained a personal, color-coded spreadsheet tracking every CSM's touches per account per week.
No one asked speaker to create this spreadsheet.

In Q3 2019, during a high-churn-risk renewal quarter, speaker put every at-risk account on a physical wall with sticky notes and stood in front of it every morning at 7:15am with whoever was in the office, reviewing accounts one by one.
Gross retention ended at approximately 94% versus a modeled 88%.
At the Christmas party, someone told speaker's wife that speaker was the reason the company didn't fall apart.
Speaker currently has a smaller wall with sticky notes at their own place.
Speaker's ops guy has tried to get speaker to switch to a digital tool instead of the wall.

patterns.title: In the one story about your own body's worst experience, you never describe your own body.
patterns.description: You call the NICU "the worst I've ever been," and you fill it with data about Crew's weight and a direct quote from Britt — but there's no sentence anywhere about your own fear, sadness, or physical state during those nineteen days. That's notable because you clearly have that muscle: "I felt sick on Wednesdays. Like physically." You used it for a sales job. You didn't use it for your son.
patterns.prediction: Mental health: in therapy, you'll describe work-related physical anxiety more easily than family-related fear, and need to be prompted to find the latter.

patterns.title: The truck-clipboard ritual with your dad is the direct ancestor of "Council" with Britt — but you've added an agenda your dad never had.
patterns.description: You said it yourself: "My dad had the truck. I've got the doc... I think it's the same thing." Your father's ritual was silent and undocumented. Yours has a shared doc, explicit categories, and — after Britt joked about it — you added a new section unprompted, turning a moment meant for closeness into one more thing you formalize. Same move as the mission board and the sales spreadsheet.
patterns.prediction: Communication: in relational tension with Britt, you'll propose adding structure (a new doc section, a scheduled check-in) instead of having the hard conversation in the moment, unstructured.

patterns.title: Your stated reason for a big decision is true — and a second, more expensive image is what you actually can't stop returning to.
patterns.description: You say you quit wrestling for the truck and the money — genuinely true, you started working Saturdays that same week — but the image you keep coming back to is your coach saying four words and not fighting for you. You say you left the startup for the underserved contractor market — also true — but the detail you keep returning to is being left off the Park City invite list, and two directors going while you didn't. The practical story holds up. It's just not the part carrying the weight.
patterns.prediction: Identity: asked directly why you left or ended something else significant, you'll give the practical reason first, then, if pressed, surface a specific slight you tracked precisely at the time.
